Results of stud- ies so far have been largely disappointing, and no drug has yet been found to be effective. However, research contin- ues,40 with many trials focusing on starting treatment in the first few hours after ischaemic stroke.41 Long-term management. Patients who have had an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack are at risk of further stroke but are also at increased risk of other cardio- vascular events, including myocardial infarction and sud- den death. Long-term treatment for secondary prevention therefore has an important role.6,42-46 All patients should be assessed for standard cardiovascular risk factors, partic- ularly hypertension, and these should be treated as appro- 1186 Cardiovascular Drugs priate (see Cardiovascular Risk Reduction, p.1164). There is some evidence that reduction of blood pressure and lip- ids reduces the risk of stroke irrespective of the presence of hypertension or hyperlipidaemia,44 and the use of ACE in- hibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists47 and statins6 has been recommended. Atrial fibrillation is a spe- cific risk factor for stroke and should also be treated (see Cardiac Arrhythmias, p.1160). Hypercoagulability may increase the risk of stroke and blood screening for poly- cythaemia, thrombocytosis, and abnormal coagulation function has been recommended. Carotid endarterectomy is of established benefit for secondary prevention in pa- tients with clinically significant carotid stenosis,6,48 but its role in primary prevention is less clear.49,50 Antithrombotic therapy may also have a specific role. Antiplatelet drugs. Long-term prophylaxis with aspirin re- duces the risk of future serious vascular events including stroke in patients who have already suffered an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack,19,45,46,51 regardless of age.52 The optimum dose is unclear; medium doses of 75 to 325 mg of aspirin daily have been most widely studied51 and an analysis of trials using aspirin over a dose range of 50 to 1500 mg daily found no relationship between dose and the reduction in risk of stroke.53 In patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy the risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and death over 3 months may be lower for those taking medium dose aspirin compared with higher doses.54 Dipyridamole is also effective,55,56 and has been used in patients unable to tolerate aspirin, but it is more effective when given with aspirin56,57 and combination therapy is now preferred.6,19,45 Clopidogrel is another alternative,58 but should not be given with aspirin since any benefit is offset by an increased risk of bleeding.59 Ticlopidine has also been used, but adverse effects are a problem and a study60 in black patients found that it was less effective than aspirin.
